bestFor: Fast, cheap text-to-image drafts and iteration where no reference photo exists
Photorealistic portraits, headshots, and editorial-style character art with natural skin and studio lighting
Legible bilingual (English/Chinese) in-image text at moderate complexity
strugglesWith: Wide artistic style diversity — it leans photorealistic even for stylized asks
Crowded scenes with multiple background people (face distortion is a known failure mode)
Very long, complex text layouts (the non-Turbo Z-Image variant handles these better)

bestFor: Photorealistic product, fashion, and editorial shots where lighting, reflections, and materials must read as physically plausible
Long, detail-dense prompts with many bound attributes (exact colors, counts, positions) that need literal, faithful following
Reference-guided generation used as a style/composition guide rather than a strict pixel edit
Masked-region edits (`flux2-inpaint`) where every unmasked pixel must be preserved exactly — the result is composited back over the original, so only the selected region actually changes
strugglesWith: Deliberately abstract, painterly, or highly stylized requests — it has a strong bias back toward photorealism and will often keep the subject photoreal even when told to go stylized
Multi-step spatial/logical reasoning ("put the object left of the red one behind the blue one") — lands mid-pack on visual-logic benchmarks
Portraits can show "Flux shine": overly smooth skin and hyper-idealized facial structure when a candid, imperfect look is wanted

bestFor: Fast, low-latency image edits (1-2 seconds) where near-Dev quality is wanted without Dev's cost/latency
Identity-preserving edits and face-swap-style reference transfer, where it outperforms comparable small/fast models
Lighter-weight multi-reference edits (logo placement, object transfer between images) on more constrained hardware/turnaround budgets
strugglesWith: Nuanced artistic/stylistic tasks — noticeably behind Krea 2 and Qwen-Image for pure style work
Occasionally odd or brittle prompt-following behavior reported by users compared to the full Dev model
No official documented maximum reference-image count, so behavior at the high end (6-8 images) is less predictable than for models with a stated ceiling

bestFor: Aesthetically cohesive, mood-driven imagery — dramatic lighting, atmosphere, and editorial/magazine-style composition read as intentional
Style-reference-driven generation across illustration, anime, watercolor, and concept-art styles
Creative-direction and marketing/fashion work where visual mood matters more than literal accuracy
strugglesWith: Legible in-image text — weakest of the covered models for text rendering, avoid for any workflow whose output needs readable typography
Complex, multi-part instructional prompts with many discrete constraints

Technical/product photography where exact specifications (dimensions, exact colors, precise geometry) must match — this workflow's bundled LoRA was trained for 1-2 references, so 3 exceeds its documented training range
Chaining more than ~3 style references — prefer 'krea2-api' below, which is Krea's own hosted model built for that

bestFor: The same aesthetic/mood-driven style-reference generation as the local Krea 2 Turbo LoRA above, but using Krea's own hosted model directly — no LoRA-training-range limitation, and each reference carries its own strength (including negative weights to push away from a reference's aesthetic)
Chaining several style references at once — the underlying node documents support for up to 10 chained references, well past the local LoRA's 1-2 trained range
Cases where 'Krea 2 Large' full-quality output (vs. the Turbo distillation used locally) is worth the added hosted latency/cost
strugglesWith: It's a paid, hosted partner node — requires separately authorized/credited Krea 2 access on the Comfy account, so it's unsuitable when the user has no such access configured

True 'Moodboards' (Krea's 250-image style-analysis feature) is NOT reachable this way — it requires a moodboard first created in Krea's own web app and referenced by UUID, which this app's own upload flow cannot produce; only the direct style_reference chain (this workflow) is buildable from user-uploaded images
Same text-rendering weakness as the local Krea 2 workflow — avoid for anything needing legible in-image typography

bestFor: Multi-image and multi-person edits that must hold composition/identity together across a back-and-forth editing session, not just a single pass
Character-identity-preserving edits from a reference portrait (clothing changes, pose changes, imaginative edits) without breaking the rest of the scene
In-image text editing/replacement in Chinese and English while preserving original font, size, and styling — strong for packaging, banners, and UI mockups
Structure-aware edits that need to preserve unchanged regions precisely (product design, spatial fidelity)
strugglesWith: Needs a lower CFG than typical diffusion defaults (around 4-5, not 7-8) — higher values introduce artifacts, so downstream prompt/parameter choices matter
Improvement over single-subject edits versus its predecessor (2509) is incremental — not a strong differentiator if the task is a simple one-subject edit
Hard-capped at 3 reference images by the TextEncodeQwenImageEditPlus node this workflow uses; do not route requests needing 4+ distinct references here

bestFor: Generating a brand-new image under strong structural control from a single prepared guide (depth map, Canny edge map, pose skeleton, or soft-edge map) rather than editing an existing photo
Depth-guided control specifically — keeps pose and facial structure most consistent among the four supported control modes (canny, soft edge, depth, pose)

One-shot photo-to-guide-to-generate shortcuts exist for pose, canny, depth, lineart, and surface-normal (the last two are an off-label but live-verified-working use of the soft-edge/depth control modes) — prefer these over the standalone extractor + generic-guide two-step when the source is a plain photo, not an already-prepared guide
strugglesWith: Anything requiring the source image's own visual identity/style, not just its structure — this is a guide-image tool, not a reference/edit tool
Preserving small in-image text or fine typography faithfully unless it is explicitly called out in the prompt
Combining more than one control type at once — the model card documents that as unsupported outside an experimental diffusers path

Narrower control-type coverage than 'qwen-fun-union-controlnet' below (4 types vs. 6+inpainting) — prefer that workflow for MLSD or scribble guides, or when a single model should also handle inpainting

bestFor: The same guide-image-driven generation as the InstantX Union ControlNet, but with broader control-type coverage: canny, HED/soft-edge, depth, pose, MLSD (straight-line/architectural), and scribble guides, plus its own inpainting mode, all from one model
Architectural, product, or interior-design guides using MLSD (straight-line) control, which the InstantX Union model does not support at all
Cases where the source guide's control type is unknown or mixed — this model's broader coverage makes it the safer default among the two Qwen union ControlNets
strugglesWith: Newer and less battle-tested than the InstantX Union model (released 2025-12/2026-02 per its versioned filename) — treat outputs with slightly more scrutiny until more real-world use accumulates
Same fundamental limits as any guide-image tool: it does not carry over the source image's own visual identity/style, only its structure
Live-verified to load and execute on this Comfy Cloud account, but not yet benchmarked head-to-head against InstantX Union for output quality on any single control type

bestFor: A third option for canny/depth/inpaint guide-driven Qwen generation, using a different mechanism than the two Union ControlNets: the guide is baked into the diffusion model itself as a patch (`QwenImageDiffsynthControlnet`/`ModelPatchLoader`), not applied as an external conditioning step
Cases where the Union ControlNets' output doesn't match the desired structural fidelity — worth trying as an alternative on the same guide image since it's an independently-trained mechanism

The inpaint variant specifically: masked-region editing baked into the model patch, then composited back over the original so unmasked pixels are preserved exactly, same guarantee as the other masked workflows
strugglesWith: Only three single-purpose patches exist (canny, depth, inpaint) — no pose, MLSD, or scribble support, unlike either Union ControlNet; route those control types to `qwen-instantx-union-controlnet` or `qwen-fun-union-controlnet` instead
Not a true ControlNet by the model's own documentation — a model patch that mimics one, so behavior can differ subtly from the Union ControlNets on the same guide

Newer, narrower community tooling with less real-world track record than the Union ControlNets — the inpaint variant's mask input in particular needed non-obvious wiring to get right (uninverted raw alpha mask, not the inverted convention the other masked workflows use), so treat any future edits to this workflow with extra care

bestFor: Dense, high-fidelity in-image text and typography — including handwriting and artistic/stylized text, a clear strength versus most competitors
Multi-source compositing from several reference images at once: product swaps, element transfer between images, while preserving depth, perspective, and lighting consistency
General subject recognition and reference fidelity when combining many distinct source photos into one coherent scene
strugglesWith: Reasoning-intensive edits that need the model to infer real-world context or learn from example-based instructions — that is Seedream 5.0's differentiator, not 4.5's
This is a paid, hosted partner node — requires separately authorized/credited Seedream access on the Comfy account, so it is unsuitable when the user has no such access configured
Exact deployment limits (resolution ceiling, aspect ratios, latency) are not fully documented by the vendor, so treat edge-case requests (extreme aspect ratios, very high resolution) cautiously

displayName: Nano Banana Pro / Gemini 3 Pro Image (hosted API)
bestFor: The best-in-class choice whenever the output needs correctly spelled, legible in-image text — short taglines through long multilingual passages, with font/texture/calligraphy control
Consistent multi-image blending and accurate identity preservation across multiple subjects at once (documented up to five people)
Practical, information-dense outputs: infographics, diagrams, multilingual localized content, high-resolution (up to 4K) print-ready output
strugglesWith: Deliberately surreal, abstract, or highly stylized prompts — it has a strong RLHF-driven bias toward realism and tends to "correct" surreal intent back toward the photorealistic median
This is a paid, hosted partner node — requires separately authorized/credited Gemini image access on the Comfy account
The exact image-count ceiling and per-surface sub-caps (objects vs. people) vary by hosting surface, so treat very high reference counts as best-effort, not guaranteed

displayName: DWPose / Canny / Lineart / Depth Anything V2 / BAE control-guide extractors
bestFor: Producing a single-purpose structural guide image (pose skeleton, edge map, lineart, depth map, or normal map) from one source photo, to feed into a ControlNet generation workflow afterward
Isolating structure/pose from a source photo when its style, color, or identity should NOT carry over into the next generation step
Deterministic, fast, single-image preprocessing — these are not generative/creative choices and should be selected only as a preparation step, not as the final output a user is asking for
strugglesWith: They do not generate a new image from a prompt at all — never select one of these when the user is asking for a finished edited or generated picture
Multi-image input is not supported — each is a single-image tool by design
Extraction quality depends entirely on the clarity of the source photo (occlusion, low contrast, or cluttered backgrounds degrade the guide)

bestFor: Increasing the resolution of an existing image 4x while sharpening detail, e.g. before printing or when the user asks to "make this bigger" / "upscale" / "higher resolution" with no other edit requested
A finishing step after a generation workflow when the user wants more detail or a larger output, not a different picture
Deterministic, prompt-free, fast — no generation model or creative interpretation involved at all
strugglesWith: Any request that also wants content changed — it cannot add, remove, or alter anything, only sharpen/enlarge what's already there. Route content changes to a generation workflow instead (possibly before or after this one)
Multi-image input is not supported — single image in, single image out
Already-low-quality or heavily compressed source images: it sharpens detail that's present, it doesn't invent detail that was lost

bestFor: Cutting a subject out onto a transparent background — "remove the background", "isolate the product/person", or prep work before compositing into another image (e.g. as a reference for one of the multi-image generation workflows)
General-purpose subjects (the bundled graph uses the isnet-general-use model); works for products, people, and most everyday objects
Deterministic, prompt-free, fast — no generation model or creative interpretation involved at all
strugglesWith: Fine, wispy detail (individual hair strands, fur, semi-transparent materials like glass or smoke) — general-purpose background removers commonly leave soft/fuzzy edges or halos on these

Any request that also wants content changed or a new background painted in — this only removes, it doesn't generate or replace; pair with a generation workflow for a full "replace the background" request
Multi-image input is not supported — single image in, single image out
